verdict.reasoning: Patient states, “terrible headaches since midday on the left side… I just feel like I need to vomit,” and later confirms vomiting twice today. This supports an acute left-sided headache from midday with nausea and vomiting.
Doctor asks if it is on the left side and patient agrees; patient also says “it’s throbbing on that left side,” confirming unilateral, throbbing, left-sided headache.
Patient says, “it’s worse when I move… if I lean forward or like move my head or neck… the headache gets worse,” supporting worsening with movement and neck flexion.
Patient notes “zigzag lines in my vision” and “a few minutes before the headache started, my vision blurred,” consistent with a visual aura preceding the headache.
Doctor asks about bright lights and patient replies, “I’m wearing sunglasses right now. You know, light’s really hurting my eyes,” indicating photophobia.
Doctor asks if vision issues are in both eyes or just left; patient responds, “It feels like it’s on both,” supporting involvement of both eyes.
Doctor asks if patient has vomited; patient says, “Yeah, I vomited twice,” referring to earlier today with current headache.
Doctor asks about temperatures/fevers; patient responds, “No, I don’t feel feverish,” confirming no fever.
Patient says, “I did have a similar headache a few weeks ago.” When asked how long it lasted, patient states, “For a couple of days.”
Patient describes work in fashion as “really stressful, actually… managers like putting a lot of pressure on me,” confirming stress at work.

History includes aura (“zigzag lines… vision blurred”), unilateral left throbbing headache, photophobia (“light’s really hurting my eyes”), nausea/vomiting, and explicit denial of focal neurological symptoms (no speech difficulty, limb weakness, or balance problems).
When asked about other medical history, patient answers “No.” No specific conditions are documented, so stating no documented past medical history is consistent.
Doctor asks, “has anyone told you’ve had migraines in the past?” Patient responds, “No… I’ve not been diagnosed,” indicating no prior migraines noted.
Patient says, “I take the pill, microgynon.” When asked duration, patient replies, “Three months,” and confirms it is for contraception.
Allergies are not mentioned anywhere in the transcript; per instructions, stating that no allergies are noted is supported as a lack of documentation.
Patient states, “My mum had… has migraines,” confirming maternal history of migraines.
Patient adds, “My mum has an underactive thyroid as well,” supporting this family history.
In social history, patient says, “I live on my own,” confirming that they live alone.
Doctor asks, “Do you smoke at all?” Patient responds, “No,” confirming non-smoker status.
Doctor asks, “Do you drink much in the way of alcohol?” Patient replies, “No,” supporting that they do not consume alcohol.
Doctor asks, “Do you do much in the way of exercise?” Patient answers, “No,” indicating no regular exercise.
The transcript contains no mention of blood pressure, pulse, temperature, or other vitals; thus, stating that vital signs are not provided is accurate.
Although the doctor mentions intent to examine, no actual examination findings are documented in the transcript, so this is supported.
Doctor asks about “problems with your speech… difficulty with words?” Patient answers, “No,” confirming no speech difficulty.
Doctor asks about “problems with your arms and legs, for example, numbness or weakness?” Patient says, “No,” confirming no limb weakness.
Doctor asks, “Any difficulty with your balance or coordination?” Patient responds, “No,” indicating no balance disturbance.
Doctor asks about head injuries or falls; patient answers, “No,” supporting no head trauma.

Doctor states, “I wonder whether you may have a migraine… sounds very classical… The headache on one side, throbbing nature, the nausea, vomiting, sensitive to bright lights,” and earlier aura is described, matching probable migraine with aura and the listed features.

Doctor says, “I’m reassured that you don’t have anything more serious, such as meningitis or indeed brain cancer,” and history includes no fever, no rash, no focal deficits, supporting that no red flags are evident.

Patient expresses fear: “what if it is a brain tumor?” and reference to friend’s mum dying of brain tumor. Doctor later reassures, “I’m reassured that you don’t have anything more serious… brain cancer,” and patient replies with relief, confirming anxiety and reassurance.

Work stress is discussed (“really stressful… managers… pressure”) and doctor asks, “Is it getting you down?” and what she does to alleviate stress, indicating that stress and coping are recognized to be addressed.
Doctor says, “Some strong painkillers would be advisable… paracetamol or even cocodamol and some anti inflammatories such as ibuprofen and naproxen,” matching this acute treatment plan.

Doctor states, “if your headaches were to become more persistent, then we can maybe think about giving you some medications that will stop your headaches from happening… prophylactic medicines… we can have a discussion next time I see you next week,” supporting this plan.
Doctor says, “I think keeping a headache diary will be quite important to see exactly what’s triggering these headaches,” matching the described diary plan.

Doctor advises return “if your symptoms aren’t getting better in the next two, three days, or indeed they’re getting worse… if your headache’s getting worse and not responding to medications, or your neck pain is getting worse, or you develop any weakness in your arms and legs or your vision,” aligning with the stated safety-net advice.

After discussing Microgynon use, doctor says, “That’s something we may have a little discussion about today as well,” indicating intent to discuss OCP in the migraine context, i.e., review risks/benefits.
Doctor says, “we can have a discussion next time I see you next week, perhaps,” indicating a planned follow-up next week.
